summary: Mobility is near normal with MF-Index 71 and PT ridership approaching pre‑pandemic levels, but fuel‑saving outcomes remain far below theoretical targets and high‑risk sectors show limited WFH adoption. Targeted policy tweaks can lock in gains and mitigate emerging economic risks.

signals.detail: The theoretical ceiling of 35.7 M litres/week translates to only 334 k litres saved in the first week of the mandate (~1% of the modelled target), indicating weak compliance despite a perfect fuel‑policy score.
Daily PT trips total 1.24 M, close to the pre‑COVID daily average (~1.43 M) and well above MCO lows, reflecting a steady rebound though still shy of historic levels.
Logistics, construction and retail show mobility scores above 85 and are classified as HIGH risk, signalling potential congestion, emissions and supply‑chain strain if WFH remains low.
WFH adoption varies sharply: 60% in public/GLCs versus 5‑15% in high‑mobility sectors, creating an equity gap that undermines the overall MF‑Index and fuels uneven economic pressure.
Fuel prices are high (RON95 RM3.87/L, diesel RM4.87/L) which could encourage a shift to PT, yet ridership has not fully capitalised on price signals, suggesting the modal shift is still tentative.

recommendation: Introduce enforceable WFH incentives for logistics, retail and construction aiming for at least 30% remote work by end‑2027, pair this with a targeted fuel‑rebate for low‑emission vehicles and accelerate PT capacity upgrades to restore daily ridership to pre‑pandemic levels within 12 months.
